summary: CODEC proposes applying sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to decompose neural network *contributions* (the composition of receptive and projective fields) rather than *activations* alone, yielding sparser, more class-discriminative modes that support network control and a dual application to retinal CNN models. The core idea is principled and the retinal neuroscience application is the paper's most distinctive element. However, the work is weakened by a critical gap in related-work positioning (the burgeoning SAE-on-activations mechanistic interpretability literature is largely absent), insufficient statistical rigor in the main experiments, an underdeveloped and self-admittedly inferior ViT section that strains the generality claim, and a primary baseline that is narrowly the authors' own activation-mode counterpart rather than competing interpretability paradigms.
strengths: Principled causal framing: computing contributions (receptive field ∘ projective field) rather than activations captures a genuine additional signal, and the argument that activations alone cannot reveal projective-field-level causality is well-motivated.

Dual application to biological and artificial networks: the retinal CNN experiment (Section 8) is distinctive, grounded in prior biological literature, and produces concrete, experimentally testable hypotheses about interneuron combinatorics and dynamic receptive fields.
Empirical finding on positive/negative decorrelation across layers (Fig. 3C–D) is novel and offers a biologically inspired interpretation linking to center-surround computations.
Practical: CODEC requires no training labels and takes only 3–7 min per layer; training-data-free interpretability methods have clear applied value.
Hyperparameter robustness analysis (Supp. Figs. S3/S4) is appreciated; most SAE papers omit this.

key_concerns.issue: Critical missing related work: the paper does not cite or compare against the extensive 2022–2024 literature on SAEs applied to activations in mechanistic interpretability (Cunningham et al. 2023; Bricken et al. 2023; Elhage et al. 2022 on superposition; Templeton et al. 2024). Since CODEC's core technical element is an SAE applied to a different object (contributions vs. activations), the contribution cannot be properly evaluated without positioning against this body of work. Reviewers will immediately notice this gap.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a dedicated subsection in Related Work that engages with the SAE mechanistic interpretability literature. Quantitatively compare CODEC modes against SAE-on-activations baselines from that literature (e.g., Cunningham et al.) using the same evaluation metrics (class correlation, ablation efficacy). The activation-mode baseline the authors already have is a step in this direction but needs to be tied to these published methods.

key_concerns.issue: Missing comparison to causal and circuit-level interpretability methods: path patching, activation patching (Meng et al. 2022 ROME; Geiger et al. causal abstraction; Wang et al. 2022 IOI circuits) and concept-based probing (NetDissect, TCAV beyond the brief mention) are the natural competing paradigms for claiming causal interpretability of intermediate layers. None appear in the experiments.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: At minimum, compare ablation/preservation accuracy (Fig. 6D) against a path-patching or activation-patching baseline. Even a discussion of why those methods are not directly comparable would suffice if a full empirical comparison is infeasible; the current paper simply ignores them.

key_concerns.issue: Statistical rigor in main experiments is insufficient: most primary results (sparsity comparisons, class-correlation histograms, ablation curves) appear to be reported without error bars, seed variance, or significance tests. R²=0.85 reconstruction accuracy is stated without justification that this threshold is adequate for downstream validity. It is unclear how many random seeds, image samples, or models are behind the curves in Figs. 5–6.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report mean ± std across at least 3 seeds for the main SAE results; add confidence intervals or bootstrap error bars to the class-correlation and ablation efficacy plots; provide a brief sensitivity analysis showing that the R²=0.85 reconstruction quality does not degrade downstream control performance.

key_concerns.issue: The ViT section (Section 9) is underdeveloped and self-undermining: the authors acknowledge 'overall ablation performance was inferior to that observed in CNNs' and that 'further exploration is needed.' This single section is the only evidence that CODEC generalises beyond CNNs, yet it explicitly fails on that architecture. Leaving it as-is weakens the generality claim in the abstract and introduction.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Either substantially strengthen the ViT analysis (develop and evaluate an appropriate spatial-reduction strategy; report quantitative comparisons at the level of CNN results) or reframe the paper's scope to CNN/feedforward architectures and move the ViT content to a clearly labelled preliminary/negative result in the Appendix.

key_concerns.issue: The contribution target (top logit) is chosen for computational convenience but is not well-justified theoretically and is not evaluated against alternatives. Top-logit attribution may bias results toward high-confidence examples and may produce qualitatively different modes for ambiguous or misclassified images.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Include a brief ablation over contribution targets (top-logit, top-k sum, entropy) showing that the main findings are robust; this is already described as available in code but not reported empirically in the main paper.

key_concerns.issue: The SAE encoder architecture (fenc) is only partially specified in the main text; the reader is sent to Supplementary Sec. 10.4 for details. For a method paper at a venue where reviewers expect reproducibility, the key architectural choices (depth, width, activation function) should appear in the main text.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a one-paragraph methods box or table in the main text with encoder architecture, threshold value τ, dictionary size, and training setup.

questions_for_authors: How does CODEC compare quantitatively to published SAE-on-activations baselines (e.g., Cunningham et al. 2023) on the class-correlation and ablation metrics you report? Is the contribution-vs-activation advantage preserved when both are run with the same SAE implementation?
For the ablation/preservation experiments (Fig. 6D–E), what are the error bars across seeds and image subsets? Is the advantage of contribution modes over activation modes statistically significant?

The R²=0.85 SAE reconstruction is treated as a fixed threshold. Have you verified that modes derived at, say, R²=0.70 or R²=0.92 yield qualitatively different downstream control results? What is the reconstruction-vs-interpretability Pareto curve?

In the ViT experiments, what specific failure mode leads to inferior ablation performance? Is it the token-as-space analogy, the lack of spatial equivariance, or something else? Have you tried any alternative spatial aggregation strategies, even informally?

The positive/negative decorrelation finding (Fig. 3C–D) is presented as unexpected. Have you ruled out the simpler explanation that this is an artifact of ReLU nonlinearities creating increasingly sparse positive activations in later layers, which would mechanically decorrelate positive and negative gradient flows?
calibration_check: The abstract and introduction claims ('cannot be determined by analyzing activations alone', 'a rich and interpretable framework', 'mechanistic insights') are moderately supported by the CNN/retina experiments but are overclaimed given the self-admitted failure on ViTs and the absence of comparison to competing mechanistic interpretability methods.

significance.justification: The contribution-vs-activation distinction is meaningful and the retinal neuroscience application is a genuine differentiator, but incremental combination of existing tools (Integrated Gradients + SAEs) limits impact without stronger comparison to the active SAE interpretability community.

novelty.justification: Applying SAEs to contributions rather than activations is a logical and interesting step, but it is an obvious next move given the existing SAE mechanistic interpretability literature, and the paper does not demonstrate awareness of that literature to properly establish the delta.

rigor.justification: Core methodology (Integrated Gradients completeness, sparsity metrics, SAE training) is technically sound, but causal claims rest largely on ablation experiments without adequate controls or comparison to alternative causal methods.

statistical_soundness.justification: Most main-text figures lack error bars or variance estimates across seeds; the R²=0.85 adequacy threshold is asserted without justification; class-correlation differences between contributions and activations are not tested for statistical significance.

calibration_honesty.justification: The ViT failure and the limitation to specific ResNet blocks are acknowledged, but the abstract makes broad generality claims ('any trained feedforward model', 'mechanistic insights') that are not yet supported at the claimed scope.

clarity.justification: The paper is generally readable and the biological-artificial framing is cohesive, but the method section is dense, the ViT section is thinly written, and Figure 3's caption appears to bleed into the main text in the extracted version, suggesting formatting issues.

structure_compliance.justification: Standard ICLR structure is followed with a dedicated Limitations section; the paper is within reasonable length bounds and the four-stage CODEC framework is clearly enumerated.

reproducibility.justification: Key hyperparameters (threshold, dictionary size, learning rate, batch size, epochs, GPU) are provided, but SAE encoder architecture is deferred to supplementary material and the contribution computation pipeline would require significant implementation effort to reproduce from the main text alone.

related_work.justification: The SAE mechanistic interpretability literature (Cunningham, Bricken, Elhage, Templeton) is entirely absent; causal tracing and path-patching methods are not discussed; concept-based methods (NetDissect, TCAV) receive only brief mentions without quantitative comparison — this is the most significant positioning failure.

figure_quality.justification: From the captions, figures appear well-designed and cover the key claims (sparsity, class correlation, ablation, retinal IRFs), with the contribution-map visualizations in Fig. 7 being particularly informative; some captions are terse and would benefit from clearer axis descriptions.

breadth_generality.justification: Experiments are concentrated on ResNet-50 with limited subset analysis; ViT results are acknowledged to be inferior; the retinal model adds breadth but is a small-scale network; no language model or other modality results are included in the main paper despite claims of architectural agnosticism.

overall_recommendation.justification: Borderline reject: the core idea has merit and the retinal application is distinctive, but blocking gaps in related-work positioning and statistical rigor require substantial revision before this is competitive with accepted ICLR interpretability papers.
